Surat Ya-Sin is Meccan. And from him (ﷺ): "It is called al-Mu'imma (the one that envelops). It envelops its companion with the good of both abodes. Al-Daf'a (the repeller) and al-Qadiya (the one that fulfils) repel from him every evil and fulfil for him every need." Its verses number eighty-three.

﴿Ya-Sin﴾ is either recited as a list of letters (ta'did, enumeration), in which case it has no place in i'rab (grammatical case inflection), or it is the name of the surah. This is what al-Khalil and Sibawayh stated, and most scholars hold it. If it is the name of the surah, its position is either raised (marfu') as the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative (mansub) as the object of a hidden verb. On these two readings rests the recitation of (Ya-Sin) with a damma and with a fatha: the meaning is "This is Ya-Sin," or "Recite Ya-Sin." It is not permissible to read it in the accusative by supposing a hidden verb of oath, because what follows it is the thing sworn by, and they have rejected combining two oaths on one matter before the first is completed. Nor is there room for it to be a conjunction, since the two differ in their i'rab. It has also been said that it is in the genitive, with the particle of oath (ba' al-qasam) omitted, and is written with a fatha because it is indeclinable, as was explained at the opening of Surat al-Baqara. This is because those of these openings that are single letters, such as Sad, Qaf and Nun, or that are balanced like a single word, such as Ta-Sin, Ya-Sin and Ha-Mim, which balance Qabil and Habil, admit verbal i'rab. Sibawayh mentioned this in the chapter on the names of the surahs in his book. It has also been said that the two are vowels of indeclinability (haraka bina'), as in "haythu" and "ayna," as the recitation of Ya-Sin with a kasra, like Jayr, testifies. It has also been said that the fatha and kasra are a way of moving to ease the pronunciation in escaping the meeting of two sukun (unvocalised letters).

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that its meaning is "O man" in the dialect of Tayy. They said that what is meant by it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Perhaps its origin is "Ya Unaysayn" (O two little people), and it was shortened to half of it, as it is said: "Man Allahi fi Aymani Allah" (the oath "Man Allah" from "Ayman Allah").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 2:

﴿And the Qur'an﴾, in the genitive case (bi'l-jarr), on the basis that it is an oath sworn by Him from the outset. It has also been permitted that it be a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿Yasin﴾, on the assumption that it is in the genitive by means of an implied particle of oath (bāʾ al-qasam). ﴿Full of wisdom﴾, that is: containing wisdom (al-mutaḍammin li'l-ḥikmah), or speaking it by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), or characterised by it through metaphorical attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī). It has also been permitted that the original reading was (al-ḥakīma qāʾiluhu, "wise is its speaker"), so the governed noun was elided and the noun in the genitive was put in its place. Then, by its becoming nominative after having been genitive, a pronoun became hidden within it in the attributive adjective (al-ṣifah al-mushabbahah), as has passed in the opening of Surah Luqman.

This is the response to the oath: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. The sentence refutes the denial of the disbelievers, who said concerning him (ﷺ): "You are not a messenger." This testimony from Him, Exalted and Majestic, is among the things alluded to by His words in reply to them: ﴿Say: God is sufficient as a witness between me and you﴾. In singling out the Qur'an as the object of the oath (qasam) first, and describing it as "the Wise" second, there is an honoring of its status and an alert that just as it bears witness to his prophethood (ﷺ) through its inimitable composition, which encompasses wondrous wisdoms, it also bears witness to it from this aspect as well. This is because swearing by something (p-159) is calling it as a witness to establishing the content of the oath-sentence and strengthening its affirmation, so it is a witness to it and a definitive proof of it.

And His words, Exalted:

"On a straight path" is either another predicate of "innaka" (indeed you), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in the prepositional phrase, on the understanding that it refers to the noble Sharia in its entirety, not to tawhid alone. Its purpose is to show that the Sharia of the Prophet (ﷺ) is the most upright and the most just of the Sharias, as indicated by the indefinite form used for magnification (al-tankir al-tafkhimi), and by the description coming right after the statement that he (ﷺ) is among the messengers who bring Sharias.

**﴿Revelation from the Mighty, the Merciful﴾** is in the accusative (*nuṣiba*) as an expression of praise (*al-madḥ*, a form of laudatory accusative). It is also read in the nominative (*raf'*), as the predicate of an omitted subject (*khabar mubtada' maḥdhūf*), and in the genitive (*jarr*), as an apposition (*badal*) to "the Qur'an." In every case it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) used in the sense of the passive participle (*bi-ma'na al-maf'ūl*), and the Qur'an is described by it. This expresses the full eminence of the Qur'an in being sent down from God, Mighty and Majestic, as though it were the very act of sending down, and it shows its grandeur in relation to Him after its intrinsic grandeur has been stated by describing it as "wise."

By specifying the two noble names, which indicate complete dominance and general compassion, there is an exhortation to belief, both through warning and through encouragement. It also conveys that its sending down arises from the utmost mercy, as expressed in the words of the Exalted: ﴿We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. It has been said that the accusative is that of an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkid*) for its implied verb, meaning: "It was sent down as the sending down of the Mighty, the Merciful." It has also been said that it is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nāf*) brought to explain the grandeur of the status of the Qur'an mentioned above. In every case, there is an additional emphasis on the content of the oath clause (*al-jumla al-qasamiyya*).

﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ متعلِّق بـ(تَنْزِيلَ) على الوجوه الأُوَل، وبعامله المضمَر (مُتعلِّق/عامِل: الفعل المحذوف الذي يتعلّق به الجار والمجرور) على الوجه الأخير، أي: لتُنذِرَ به، كما في صدر الأعراف. وقيل: هو متعلِّق بما يدل عليه (لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ)، أي: إنك مُرسَلٌ لِتُنذِرَ ﴿قَوْمًا ما أُنْذِرَ آباؤُهُمْ﴾، أي: لم يُنذَر آباؤهم الأقربون لتطاوُل مدة الفَتْرة (الفترة: المدة الفاصلة بين الرسل). وذلك على أنّ "ما" نافيةٌ (ما: حرف نفي)، فتكون صفةً مبيِّنةً لغاية احتياجهم إلى الإنذار. أو أنّ "ما" الذي أُنذَرَه، أو شيئًا أنذره آباؤهم الأبعدون، وذلك على أنها موصولة (بمعنى "الذي") أو موصوفة (بمعنى "شيء")، فيكون مفعولًا ثانيًا لـ(تُنْذِرَ). أو: إنذارَ آبائهم الأقدمين، على أنها مصدرية (تُؤوَّل مع الفعل بمصدر)، فيكون نعتًا لمصدرٍ مؤكِّدٍ، أي: لتُنذِرَ إنذارًا كائنًا مثلَ إنذارهم.

﴿فَهم غافِلُونَ﴾: على الوجه الأول، يتعلّق بنفي الإنذار المترتِّب عليه، والضمير للفريقين، أي: لم تُنذَر آباؤهم، فهم جميعًا لأجله غافلون. وعلى الوجوه الباقية يتعلّق بقوله تعالى: "لِتُنذِرَ"، أو بما يفيده (إنك لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ)، وهو وارد لتعليل إنذاره (ﷺ) أو إرساله بغفلتهم المُحوِجة إليهما. وعلى أنّ الضمير للقوم خاصةً، فالمعنى: فهم غافلون عنه، أي: عمّا أُنذِر آباؤهم الأقدمون، لامتداد المدة. و"اللام" في قوله تعالى:

﴿Indeed the word has come into effect against most of them﴾ is the answer to the oath, meaning: By Allah, it has certainly been established and confirmed against them without exception. However, this is not by way of compulsion (jabr), without anything from their side that would call for it. Rather, it is due to their persistence, by their own choice, in disbelief and denial; their lack of response to admonition and warning; their extreme obstinacy and transgression; and their persistence in following the steps of Satan, to the extent that no turning-away diverts them and no inclination bends them. How could it not be so? And what is meant by "the word that has come" is His saying, exalted is He, to Iblis when he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with the jinn and mankind, all together﴾, as indicated by the mention of the jinn before mankind. For, as you see, he has placed the ruling upon them by bringing Hell upon those who followed Iblis, and this is definitively a justification for it by their following him. The confirmation of the word upon these, whom He referred to as "most of them," is only because they are among those who persistently insist on following Iblis forever. Since it has become clear that the basis for the word's establishment and its being realized against them is their persistence in disbelief until death, it becomes evident that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is in reality a consequence of that, not of the establishment of the word.

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, We have put shackles on their necks﴾ This is an affirmation of their determination upon disbelief and their refusal to desist from it, by depicting their condition as that of those whose necks have been fettered. ﴿So they are up to the chins﴾ That is: the shackles reach up to their chins, so they do not let them turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks toward it, nor lower their heads before it. ﴿So they are raised-up [heads]﴾ meaning raising their heads, lowering their gaze, such that they can hardly see the truth, or look in its direction.

﴿And We have set before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they cannot see﴾. This is either a continuation of the simile and completes it in the fullest sense, meaning: "And We have placed, in addition to what has been mentioned, a great barrier before them and a similar barrier behind them, and We have covered their sight with them, so that because of this they are not at all able to see anything." Or it is a separate simile. What has been mentioned, namely their being confined between two terrifying barriers which have covered their sight so that they see nothing at all, is sufficient to reveal the extreme horror of their state, and that they are imprisoned in the pit of error and ignorance, deprived of reflecting upon the proofs and signs.

It was recited as (سُدًّا) with a *damma*, which is a dialectal variant of the same word. It was said: what is the work of people is with a *fatha*, and what is the creation of God is with a *damma*. It was also recited as (فَأعْشَيْناهُمْ), from *al-'asha* (weakness of sight). It was said: the two verses concern the Banu Makhzum. Abu Jahl swore that if he saw the Messenger of God ﷺ praying, he would crush his head. He came to him while he, ﷺ, was praying, carrying a stone to smash him with it. When he raised his hand, his hand became bent up to his neck, and the stone stuck to his hand until they freed it from him with difficulty. He returned to his people and informed them of this. Another man of Makhzum said: "I will kill him with this stone." He went, and God the Exalted blinded his sight.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 10:

﴿And it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. This is an explicit statement of their condition, following its illustration by way of metaphor (tamthil). That is: their being warned by you and not being warned are equal to them, as its verification has passed in Surah al-Baqarah. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they will not believe﴾, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that emphasizes what precedes it and clarifies the ambiguity (ijmal) in what the equality concerns; or it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal) for it; or it is a substitute (badal) for it. Since it was made clear that the warning is to them like its absence, it was followed by an explanation of who is affected by it, so it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, you only warn﴾ — that is, a warning that is followed by its effect — ﴿whoever follows the Reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an, by reflecting upon it, or by admonition, and does not persist in following the steps of Satan, ﴿and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾. That is: (p-161) he fears His punishment while being absent from him (i.e., while He is unseen by him). This may be taken as a circumstantial clause (hal, a grammatical state) relating either to the subject (the one who fears) or to the object (the Merciful). Or it means that he fears Him in his inner self (sariraḥ, his innermost heart), and is not deceived by His mercy, for He is the Avenger, the Subduer, just as He is the Merciful, the Forgiving, as expressed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾. ﴿So give him good tidings of forgiveness﴾, great, ﴿and a generous reward﴾, whose worth cannot be measured. The "fa'" (so/then) indicates the sequence of the good tidings, or the command to give them, upon what precedes it of following the Reminder and fear (of Allah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾ is an explanation of a great matter that encompasses warning and good tidings in a general way, i.e., We resurrect them after their death. And it is related from al-Hasan: their "giving life" is their being brought out of polytheism (shirk) into faith (iman). In that case it is a noble promise of the realization of what was given as glad tidings. ﴿And We record what they have sent forward﴾, i.e., what they have put forward of righteous deeds and others, ﴿and their traces﴾ which they have left behind of good works, such as knowledge they taught, or a book they composed, or an endowment (habis) they established, or a building they erected, such as mosques, hostels (ribat) and bridges (qanatir), and other forms of righteousness.

And of the evil deeds, such as establishing laws of injustice and aggression, and arranging the foundations of evil and corruption among people, and other kinds of wrongdoing that they invented and instituted for those of the corrupters who came after them.

It has been said: they are the traces of those who walk to the mosques, and perhaps the intended meaning is that they are among the traces. It is also read as ﴿wayuktabu﴾ (and is written) in the passive voice, with ﴿athārahum﴾ in the nominative case. ﴿And every thing﴾, of whatever kind it may be, ﴿We have enumerated in a clear Imam﴾, a fundamental record of great importance that makes manifest all things that have occurred and that will occur, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It is also read as ﴿kullu shay'in﴾ with the nominative case.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 13:

﴿And present to them the example of the people of the town﴾. Ḍarb al-mathal (presenting a parable, lit. "striking a likeness") is used at times to apply a strange situation to another similar situation, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God presents as an example for those who disbelieve the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾. And at other times it is used to mention a strange situation and explain it to people without intending to apply it to a counterpart, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have set forth for you the parables﴾, according to one of the two interpretations, meaning: We have explained to you wondrous conditions that are, in their strangeness, like parables.

So the meaning according to the first usage is: make the people of the town an example for these people in their extremism in disbelief and their persistence in denying the messengers. That is, apply their condition to theirs, on the basis that "mathalan" is the second object of "iḍrib" and "aṣḥāba al-qaryah" is its first object, which has been placed after it so that what explains and clarifies it is joined to it.

And according to the second usage: mention and explain to them a story that is, in its strangeness, like the parable. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the people of the town﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it, with an elided noun (taqdīr al-muḍāf), or it is an explanation (bayān) of it. The qaryah (town) is Antioch. ﴿When the messengers came to it﴾ is a badal ishtimāl (inclusive substitute) for "the people of the town." They were the messengers of ʿĪsā (ﷺ)... to its people, and the attribution of their sending to Him, Exalted is He, in His saying:

(p-162) "When We sent to them two" [messengers]. This is on the basis that it was by His command, exalted is He, in order to complete the parable and to complete the consolation. The two were Yahya and Bulus. It was also said that they were other than these two. "But they denied them," meaning: they came to them and invited them to the truth, but [the people] denied them regarding the message. "Then We strengthened [them]," meaning: We reinforced them. It is said: "The rain strengthened (ʿazzaza) the earth" when it packed it down, and it was read with a light vowel as ʿazaha, from ʿazza (to overpower and subdue), when he overcame and dominated him. The object is omitted because what precedes it indicates it, and because the purpose is to mention that by which they were strengthened. "With a third," who was Shamʿun. "They said," meaning: all of them together, "Indeed we are sent to you," emphasizing their statement because of the prior denial, since denying the two is denying the third, given the unity of their word. The reason is that they were worshippers of idols, so ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) sent two to them. When they drew near to the city, they saw an old man tending his small flock, who was Habib al-Najjar, the companion of Yasin. He asked them and they informed him. He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "We heal the sick, and we cure the blind and the leper." He had a son who had been sick for two years, so they wiped over him and he stood up, and Habib believed. The news spread, and a multitude was cured at their hands. Their report reached the king, and he said to them: "Do we have a god besides our gods?" They said: "Yes, the one who brought you into existence and your gods." He said: "I will look into your matter." The people followed them. It was said that they were beaten, and it was said that they were imprisoned. Then ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) sent Shamʿun, who entered disguised and kept company with the king's retinue until they became familiar with him, and they raised his news to the king, who became fond of him. One day he said to him: "It has reached me that you imprisoned two men; have you heard what they say?" He said: "No, anger prevented me from that." So [the king] summoned them. Shamʿun said: "Who sent you?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." He said: "Describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills, and judges what He desires." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "What does the king wish for?" So he summoned a boy whose eyes were blinded, and they called upon God, exalted is He, until sight split open for him. They took two pellets and placed them in his eyeballs, and they became two eyes with which he saw. Shamʿun said to him: "Do you see? If you asked your god to do the like of this, it would be for you and for him a distinction?" He said: "I have no secret from you. Indeed our god neither sees nor hears, neither harms nor benefits." Shamʿun used to enter with them upon the idol, pray, and humble himself, and they supposed he was one of them.

Then he said: "If your god is able to bring a dead man to life, we will believe in Him." So they called for a boy who had died seven days earlier, and he stood up and said: "I was made to enter seven valleys of fire, and I warn you of what you are in, so believe!" He said: "The gates of heaven were opened and I saw a youth of beautiful face interceding for these three." The king said: "Who are they?" He said: "Shamʿun and these two." The king was amazed. When Shamʿun saw that his words had affected him, he advised him, and he believed, and a people believed. Whoever did not believe, Jibril (peace be upon him) shouted at them and they perished. Thus they said, but the context of the noble arrangement does not support this, since it is limited to relating their persistence in obstinacy and contention and their riding upon the back of arrogance in dispute, and no one is mentioned in it as believing except Habib. Had the king and a group of his retinue believed, it would be apparent that they would have supported the messengers and aided them, whether they were accepted in that or killed, like the martyr-like conduct of the carpenter (al-Najjar), and there would have been some mention of them in some way. Unless the king's belief was secret, out of fear of the arrogant leaders of his council, so that he withdrew from them, making an excuse of some kind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 15:

﴿They said﴾ i.e., the people of Antioch who did not believe, addressing the three [messengers]: ﴿You are but humans like us﴾ without any distinction in you over us that would make it fitting for you to be singled out with what you claim. The raising of (basharun, "humans") is because the negation, which would call for the operation of (ma) through (illa) [i.e., for ma to govern the predicate in the accusative], has been broken [by the illa]. ﴿And the Most Merciful has not sent down anything﴾ of what you claim of revelation and messengership. ﴿You are only lying﴾ in your claim to be messengers.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 36, verse 16:

﴿They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you."﴾

They invoked the knowledge of God, the Exalted, and this functions in the manner of an oath (qasam), together with the warning it contains against contradicting the knowledge of God, the Exalted. They also added the emphatic lam (al-lam al-mu'akkidah), because of the intense denial they had witnessed from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 17:

﴿And upon us is nothing﴾, i.e., on the part of our Lord, ﴿except the clear conveyance﴾, i.e., nothing but the conveying of His message in a manifest and clear manner (p-163) through the signs that bear witness to its truth. We have discharged this duty, so there is no blame upon us after this on the part of our Lord. Or it means: there is nothing upon us that we are held to account for on your part, except conveying the message in the manner mentioned, and we have done that. So what do you want from us, that you should believe us in this?

"They said": when their stratagems were exhausted and their pleas had failed them, ﴿Indeed, we see an omen in you﴾, that is, we consider you a bad omen (tasha'amna bikum), following the custom of the ignorant, who would take as auspicious everything that accords with their desires, even if it brings about every evil and calamity, and take as inauspicious whatever does not accord with them, even if it entails the happiness of both abodes. Or it is based on the fact that the call (to faith) is never free of warning them of something they dislike, namely the affliction of harm connected to their persons, their families and their property, should they not believe; so they shunned it. It is also related that rain was withheld from them, and so they said this (tatayyur, "augury" or "taking omen", is the term for regarding an event as an ill omen).

﴿Indeed, if you do not desist﴾, that is, from this your saying, ﴿we will surely stone you﴾ with stones, ﴿and a painful punishment from us will surely touch you﴾, the extent of which cannot be measured.

They said: "Your omen is with you." (Meaning:) the cause of your misfortune is with you, not from us, and it is your corrupt belief and the ugliness of your deeds. It is also read as "ṭayrukum" (طَيْرُكُمْ). "Is it because you were admonished?" (Meaning:) you were advised with that in which your happiness lies. The answer to the conditional (sharṭ) is omitted, relying on what precedes it as evidence for it. That is, you took bad omen and threatened (him) with stoning and torture. It is also read with an alif between the two hamzas, and with "an" (أنْ) pronounced with a fatḥah, meaning "Do you take bad omen because you were admonished?" It is also read as "wa-an dhukkirtum" (وَأنْ ذُكِّرْتُمْ), "wa-in dhukkirtum" (وَإنْ ذُكِّرْتُمْ) without the interrogative, and "wa-ayna dhukkirtum" (وَأيْنَ ذُكِّرْتُمْ), meaning: your omen is with you wherever your mention has taken place, and this is more eloquent. "Nay, you are a people who exceed limits." This is an idrab (a turning away from, or shift in, the statement) from what the conditional structure (al-shartiyyah) implies, namely that the admonition is the cause of misfortune or the justification for the threat. That is, the matter is not so; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess in disobedience, and therefore misfortune has come upon you, or (you are a people whose habit is excess) in wrongdoing and transgression, and therefore you threatened and took bad omen from one whom it is obligatory to honor and seek blessing from.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 20:

﴿And there came running from the farthest part of the city a man﴾. He was Habib al-Najjar, who used to carve their idols, and he was among those who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and between them was six hundred years. Likewise Tubba' al-Akbar (the Great Tubba'), Waraqa ibn Nawfal and others believed in him, and no one believed in any prophet other than him (ﷺ) before his mission. It is also said: he was in a cave worshipping Allah Most High, and when news of the messengers (peace and blessings be upon them) reached him, he manifested his religion. ﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), which came as an answer to a question arising from the narration of his coming running. As if it was said: "What did he say upon his coming?" So it was said: he said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾. He drew attention to the title of their mission, urging them to follow them, just as addressing them with "O my people" is to win their hearts and incline them towards accepting his advice.

And the words of the Most High:

Follow those who ask you no reward and who are guided.

This is a repetition for emphasis, and a means of describing them with what encourages people to follow them: their being free of worldly aims, and their being guided to the good of this world and the religion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 22:

﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾ This is a gentle manner of guidance (talaṭṭuf fī al-irshād), by presenting it in the setting of counsel for himself (fī ma'raḍ al-munāṣaḥah li-nafsih), and in sincere advice (imḥāḍ al-nuṣḥ), since he shows them that he chooses for them what he chooses for himself. The intent is a rebuke of them for abandoning the worship of their Creator in favor of worshipping other than Him, as its statement indicates: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, as an exaggeration in warning (mubālaghatan fī al-tahdīd). Then he returned to the first line of discourse and said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 23:

﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ It is a denial and negation of taking gods at all (ittikhadh al-alihah 'ala al-itlaq). His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿If the Most Merciful should intend for me some harm, their intercession will avail me nothing﴾, that is: it will not benefit me with any benefit, ﴿nor can they save me﴾ from that harm by helping and supporting, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for the aforementioned negation. Making it a qualifier of (gods) (alihah), as some have gone to, may perhaps give the impression that there are gods which are not like this. It was also read: (in yuridni) with a fatha on the ya', in the sense of ﴿if He makes me a channel (mawrid) of harm﴾, that is: makes me a place where harm arrives (mawrid lil-darr).

﴿Indeed, then﴾ meaning: if I were to take gods besides Him, ﴿I would certainly be in clear error﴾, for associating with Him that which has no share in benefiting, nor in averting harm, [when compared] with the Creator, the Almighty, besides whom there is no one capable, and there is no good except His good, is a manifest error that is not hidden from anyone who has discernment at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord.﴾ This is an address from him to the messengers, by way of talwin (shifting of address). It is said: when he advised his people with what has been mentioned, they resolved to stone him, so he hastened toward the messengers before they could kill him, and said that. He emphasized it only to show that it issued from him with complete desire and eagerness. He attributed the Lord to their pronoun as a gesture (rawm) toward increasing the affirmation, and to show exclusivity and emulation of them, as if he said: "By your Lord who sent you, or the One to whom you call us to believe." ﴿So hear me!﴾ That is: hear my faith, and bear witness for me before God Most High to it. It is also said: the address is to the disbelievers; he addressed them directly with that to show steadfastness in religion and indifference to being killed. The attribution of the Lord to their pronoun serves to affirm the truth and to alert to the falsehood of what they held, namely taking idols as lords. It is also said: the address is to all people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 26:

﴿It was said: "Enter Paradise."﴾ It was said to him this when they had killed him, as an honour to him by entering it then, like the rest of the martyrs (shuhada'). It was also said: when they intended to kill him, God, exalted is He, raised him up to Paradise; this is what al-Hasan said. And from Qatada: God caused him to enter Paradise, and he is in it alive, being provided for. It was also said: its meaning is the good news (bushra) of entering Paradise, and that he is among its people. And it was not said "to him" because the purpose is to state what was said (al-maqul), not the one it was said to (al-maqul lahu), since it is evident; and for the sake of emphasis on hastening to declare it.

The sentence is a resumed statement (isti'naf) that came as an answer to a question arising from the narration of his state and his speech, as if it were said: What was his meeting with his Lord after that steadfastness in his religion and his sacrifice of his soul for the sake of His face, exalted is He? So it was said: "It was said: Enter Paradise." Likewise is the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said: "Would that my people knew"﴾.

﴿Because of what my Lord has forgiven me and made me one of the honored ones.﴾ This is an answer to a question that arises from the narration of his situation, as if it were said: "What did he say upon attaining that noble honor?" So it was said: "He said" ... etc. He wished that his people knew his condition so that this would keep them from acquiring the like of it by repenting of disbelief and entering faith and obedience, following the practice of the friends of God (awliya') in restraining anger and showing mercy to enemies. Or so that they would know that they had been in great error regarding his affair, that he was upon the truth, and that their enmity had brought him nothing but happiness. It was also read as (مِنَ المُكَرَّمِينَ) (min al-mukarramīn, with the doubled rāʼ, "from among the honorers"). The word "مَا" (mā) is either relative (mawṣūla, "that which") or verbal-masdar (maṣdariyya, "that"), and "الباء" (al-bāʼ, "by/for") is a complement of "يَعْلَمُونَ" (yaʻlamūn, "they know"). Or it is interrogative (istifhāmiyya, "what?"), used in its original form, and then "الباء" is connected to "غَفَرَ" (ghafara, "forgave"), meaning: "for what did my Lord forgive me?" By this he intends to magnify the matter of his emigration from their religion and his steadfastness in enduring their harm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 28:

﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him⁠—﴾ after his killing or his raising up ⁠—﴿any host from the heaven.﴾ To destroy them and take vengeance upon them, as We did on the Day of Badr and the Trench. Rather, We sufficed in their affair with a single cry from an angel. In this there is a belittling of them with regard to their destruction, and an allusion to magnifying the station of the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And We are not those who send down⁠﴾ — and it was not fitting in Our wisdom that We should send down a host from the heaven to destroy his people. This is because We have decreed a cause for everything, since We destroyed some of the nations We destroyed by a violent wind, some by the cry, some by the earth swallowing them up, and some by drowning. We made the sending down of hosts one of your distinctions in gaining victory over your people. It has also been said that "mā" is a relative pronoun conjoined to "jund" (host), meaning: and We did not send down upon those before them stones, wind, heavy rains, and others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 29:

﴿It was but one single Cry﴾ i.e., the seizing or the punishment was nothing but ﴿one single Cry﴾ which Jibril (peace be upon him) cried out with. It is also read (ilLa sayhatun) with the nominative, on the basis that kana (was) is complete (taamma, i.e., meaning "to occur" or "to exist"). It is also read (illa zaqyatan wahidatan), from zaqa al-ta'ir (the bird chirped), meaning when it cries out. ﴿Then behold, they were extinguished﴾ i.e., dead. They were likened to an extinguished fire, as a symbol that the living is like a blazing fire in movement and flame, while the dead is like ash, as Labid said:

؎ Man is but like a shooting star and its light; it turns to ash after it was blazing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 30:

﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ Come, for this is one of the states in which you ought to be present, and it is what the words of Him, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿There never comes to them a messenger but they used to mock him.﴾ Indeed, those who mock the advisers, whose counsel is bound up with the happiness of both abodes, are deserving of being made to feel regret, and those who feel regret should grieve over them. Or the angels and the believers among the two groups (jinn and humankind) have lamented their condition. It has also been allowed that it is a lamentation over them on the part of God, exalted is He, by way of metaphor, to magnify what they have inflicted upon themselves. This is supported by the reading (yā ḥasratā), because the meaning is "O my lamentation." Its being in the accusative is due to its length, because of the prepositional phrase attached to it. It has been said that it is governed by an implied verb, and the vocative particle is omitted. It has also been read (yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād), with the noun in the genitive by being in construct with the subject or the object. And (yā ḥasratan ʿalā al-ʿibād) is with the pause treated as a continuation (ijrāʾ al-waṣl majrā al-waqf).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 31:

﴿Have they not seen﴾, i.e., have they not known? It is suspended from acting (ta'liq 'an al-'amal) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, because (kam) does not take as its operator what precedes it, even though it is declarative (khabariyyah), since its original form is interrogative (istifham), except that its meaning takes effect in the sentence, just as it takes effect in your saying: "Did you not see that Zayd is surely departing?" even though it does not govern its wording. ﴿That they (p-166) to them do not return﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "how many We destroyed" in meaning, i.e., have they not seen the abundance of Our destruction of those before them from those mentioned just now and from others, that they do not return to them? It was also read with a kasra as a resumptive (isti'naf) clause. It was also read: "Have they not seen whom We destroyed," and the substitution then is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 32:

﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us, present.﴾ This is an explanation of the return of all of them to the place of assembly (al-mahshar), after the explanation that they will not return to the worldly life (al-dunya). "In" (inna) is negating, the tanwin on "kullun" is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted after it, "lamma" is in the sense of "illa" (except), "jami'un" is on the pattern of "fa'il" in the sense of "maf'ul" (passive), and "ladayna" is an adverbial complement (zarf) either to it or to what follows it. The meaning is: "None of them but will be gathered before Us, brought forward present for reckoning and recompense." It has also been said: "muhdarun" means "those who will be punished," so "kull" is an expression for the disbelievers. It has been recited as "lamma" with the light (takhfif) form, on the basis that "in" is a lightened form of the heavy (thaqilah) "inna," the "lam" is a distinguishing particle (lam al-fariqah), and "ma" is an added particle for emphasis. The meaning is that all of them are gathered... etc.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 33:

﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ — with light stress (takhfif); it is also read with the doubled consonant (tashdid). His saying, Exalted is He, "āyatun" (sign) is a predicate placed before its subject (khabar muqaddam), for the sake of emphasis on it, and its indefiniteness (tankir) is for magnification (tafkhim). "Lahum" (for them) may be connected to it, because it means a sign (ʿalāma), or to an implied element that is an attribute of it. "Al-ard" (the earth) is the subject (mubtada'), and "al-maytah" (dead) is its attribute. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We have brought it to life﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining how it is a sign. It has also been said: "āyatun" is the subject, "lahum" is the predicate, and "al-ard al-maytah" is a described subject, whose predicate is "aḥyaynāhā," and the clause explains "āyatun." It has also been said: "al-ard" is the subject, "aḥyaynāhā" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "āyatun." It has also been said: the predicate of it is "al-ard," and "aḥyaynāhā" is its attribute, because what is meant by it is the genus and not a specific one. The first view is the preferable one, because the locus of the benefit is that the earth is a sign for them, not that the sign is the earth. ﴿And We have brought forth from it grain﴾, the genus of grain, ﴿and from it they eat﴾. The fronting of the relative complement (taqdim al-silah) serves to indicate that grain is the bulk of what is eaten and by which one sustains life.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 34:

﴿And We placed in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾ i.e., of the kinds of palm tree and grapevine. For this reason, both were given in the plural (jannat, "gardens") rather than the grain (habb), since a term denoting a genus (jins) implies difference (ikhtilaf), whereas a term denoting kinds (anwa') does not. The mention of palm trees (nakhil) rather than dates (tumur) is so that it corresponds with the grain (habb) and the grapevines (a'nab), because their trees are distinguished by greater benefit and by the traces of divine craftsmanship. ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾ — it is also read with the lightened form (tukhfif). Fajr (to cause to gush) and tafjir (to cause to gush forth intensively) are like fath (to open) and taftih (to open thoroughly), both in wording and meaning. ﴿From the springs﴾ i.e., some of the springs; the modified noun has been elided and the attribute (sifah) placed in its stead, or "al-'uyun" is meant with "min" being superfluous (mazidah) according to the view of al-Akhfash.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 35:

﴿That they may eat of its fruit﴾ is connected to (ja'alna, "We made"), and its placement after "the springs gush forth" is because it belongs to the beginnings of the fruiting, meaning: and We made therein gardens of palm trees, and We arranged the beginnings of their fruiting, ﴿that they may eat of the fruit of what has been mentioned﴾ of the gardens and the palm trees. This is with the pronoun treated in the manner of a demonstrative (ism al-isharah). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted, by way of iltifat (shift) to the third person (ghaybah), and the attribution is because God, Exalted, creates the fruit. It has been read with two dammas (thamarihi, as thumurihi), which is a dialect form of it, or it is the plural of thimar (fruits). And with one damma and a sukun (thamrihi). ﴿And what their hands have made﴾ is a conjunction over "its fruit," and it refers to what is made from it of juice (asir) and date syrup (dibs) and the like. It has been said that "ma" is a negation particle, and the meaning is that the fruit is by God's creation, not by their action; the place of the clause is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The reading (عَمِلَتْ) without a ha' (pronoun) confirms the first meaning, since omitting the returning pronoun from the relative clause is better than omitting it from other than the relative clause. ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ is a rebuke and a condemnation of their not being grateful for the countless blessings; the fa' (then) is for conjunction over an implied element required by the context, meaning: do they see these blessings, or do they enjoy them and yet not give thanks for them?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 36:

﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought forward to declare Him exalted above what they did, namely their neglect of giving Him thanks for His aforementioned bounties, and to magnify what was mentioned in the relative clause of the marvellous traces of His power, the secrets of His wisdom, and the wondrous blessings that call for gratitude and for devoting worship to Him alone, and to express wonder at their failure to do so while in such a state.

"Subhana" (Glory be to Him) is a proper noun used for tasbih (glorifying, i.e., declaring far removed from evil), which is distancing oneself from evil in belief and in speech, that is, believing in His remoteness from it and judging Him to be so. It derives from "sabaha fi al-ard wa al-ma'" (he swam/travelled far and deep in the land and the water) when he went far and deep into them; from this comes "faras sabuh" (a horse that runs widely), meaning one with a wide gait. Its position is as a verbal noun (masdar), and its governing verb is hardly ever mentioned; the sense is "I glorify Him (usabbihu subhanahu)," that is, "I declare Him exalted above what is unfitting for Him in belief and in action, with an exaltation specific to Him and befitting His majesty." There is intensification in it from the standpoint of derivation from sabh, from the standpoint of its transfer to the pattern taf'il, and from the standpoint of its departure from the verbal noun, which denotes the category, to a noun that is uniquely assigned to Him, especially a proper noun pointing to a reality present in the mind, and from the standpoint of its standing in the place of the verbal noun together with the verb. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun like "ghufran," intended to mean complete exaltation and total distance from evil, so there is intensification in attributing the exaltation to the Holy Essence. The meaning, then, is: He is exalted by His very essence above everything unfitting for Him, with an exaltation specific to Him. On this view the sentence is a report from God, Exalted is He, of His exaltation and freedom from everything unfitting for Him, both what they did and what they left undone. On the first view it is a judgement from Him, Mighty and Majestic, to that effect, and an instruction to the believers that they should say it, believe its content, not neglect it, and not be heedless of it.

By "al-azwaj" (the pairs) is meant the kinds and types. ﴿From what the earth brings forth﴾ is an explanation of them, meaning everything that grows in it of the things mentioned and others. ﴿And from themselves﴾ means He created the pairs from themselves, that is, the male and the female. ﴿And from what they do not know﴾ means and pairs from what God Exalted has not made them aware of in its particularities, since they lack the capacity to comprehend them. Since nothing of their religious or worldly interests depends on that, and He informed them of it only in summary fashion, in the manner of His saying: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾, [He did so] because their grasp of His great power and the vastness of His dominion and sovereignty depends on it.

Qur'an 36:37: ﴿And a sign for them is the night.﴾ This is a clause consisting of a predicate placed before its subject (khabar muqaddam, "fronted predicate") and a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), as has passed. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We strip from it the day﴾ is a clause explaining the manner in which it is a sign, i.e., We remove it and uncover it from its place. It is a metaphor borrowed from salkh (skinning, "stripping"), which is the removal of the connection between the animal and its hide. The more common usage ties it to the hide: one says "salakht al-ihab min al-shah" (I skinned the hide off the sheep), though it may be used in reverse, and from this comes "al-shah al-maslukhah" (the skinned sheep). ﴿Then, behold, they are in darkness﴾, i.e., they enter into darkness suddenly. In this there is an allusion (ramz) to the fact that the original state is darkness and that light is an accident (arid).

﴿And the sun runs on to a stopping place for it﴾: to a specific limit at which its course ends. It is likened to the resting place of a traveler when he has completed his journey. Or it refers to the zenith of the sky, for its movement there is found to be slowest, so that it is thought to have a pause there. He said:

؎ The sun is bewildered, spinning in the air

Or it refers to a fixed course it follows, or to a determined end for each day among the risings and settings. For it has three hundred and sixty risings and settings in its cycle. It rises each day from one rising point and sets at one setting point, and then does not return to those two until the following year. Or it refers to the cessation of its motion at the ruin of the world.

It was read as (إلى مُسْتَقَرٍّ لَها) ("to a stopping place for it"), and it was read as (لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها) ("it has no stopping place"), meaning it has no rest, for it is always in motion. It was also read as (لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها) with "لا" in the sense of لَيْسَ ("is not"), so that it means "it has no stopping place."

﴿That﴾ refers to its running, and the distance implied in it, despite the recency of the reference, is to indicate the loftiness of its rank and the greatness of its station. That is: that wondrous running, which contains splendid wisdoms that minds and understandings are bewildered in grasping. ﴿The decree of the Almighty﴾, the Victorious, who prevails by His power over every thing that can be decreed, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, whose knowledge encompasses every thing known.

﴿وَالْقَمَرَ قَدَّرْنَاهُ﴾ is in the accusative (*nasb*), governed by an implied verb that the explicit verb explains. It was also read in the nominative (*raf'*), as the subject of a nominal sentence (*ibtida'*, the inchoative construction), meaning: "We have measured for it ﴿stations﴾." It was said: "We measured its course into stations." It was said: "We made it one possessing stations." These stations are twenty-eight: al-Sharatayn, al-Butan, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hak'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, al-Ghafr, al-Zibaniyy, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, Far' al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Far' al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar, and al-Rishā', which is the belly of the fish. Each night the moon descends into one of them, neither passing beyond it nor falling short of it. When it reaches the last of its stations, which is just before the conjunction (*ijtima'*), it becomes thin and curved (*daqqa wa-istaqwasa*), ﴿until it returns like the old date-stalk﴾, that is, like the curved spathe-stalk (*al-shimrakh al-mu'awwaj*). The word *'urjūn* is of the pattern *fu'lūn*, derived from *al-in'irāj*, which means crookedness (*al-i'wijāj*). It was also read as *al-'irjūn*, and the two are dialectal variants, like *al-buzyūn* and *al-bizyūn*.

﴿الْقَدِيمِ﴾: the old, the aged (*al-'atīq*). It was said: it is that over which a year has passed or more.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 40:

﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾, i.e., it is not fitting or feasible (يَصِحُّ ويَتَسَهَّلُ) for it ﴿to overtake the moon﴾ in the speed of its course, for that would disrupt the growth of plants and the living of animals. Or [it refers to] their effects and benefits, or [to] place, namely that the sun would descend into the moon's station or its dominion and thereby obliterate its light. The placing of the negative particle (حَرْفِ النَّفْيِ) before "the sun" indicates that they are subjugated (مُسَخَّراتٌ), so that nothing is made easy for them except what has been decreed for them. ﴿Nor does the night outpace the day﴾, i.e., it does not precede it and thereby leave it behind, but it follows it in succession (يُعاقِبُهُ). It was also said that what is meant by "them" is their signs, namely the two luminaries (النَّيِّرانِ), and that by "outpacing" is meant the moon's advance into the sun's dominion, which makes it the reverse of the first case. The mention of "outpacing" in place of "overtaking" is because it is more suited to the swiftness of its motion. ﴿And each﴾, i.e., and all of them, with the tanwin (تَنْوِينَ, nunation) being a substitute (عِوَضٌ) for the genitive noun that was omitted, which is the pronoun referring to the sun and the moon. The plural is used in view of the multiplicity that accrues to them through the multiplicity of their risings, for the difference of states necessitates a certain plurality in the essence. Or it refers to the stars, since the mention of the two implies them. ﴿In an orbit they swim﴾, i.e., they travel with ease and smoothness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 41:

﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾ — their children, whom they send out with their trade goods — or their infants and their women whom they take along with them, for the term "dhurriyyah" (offspring) applies to them as well, especially when they are mixed together; and singling them out for mention is because settling them in the ships is more difficult, and holding on to them within it is more wondrous ﴿in the laden ship﴾, i.e., the filled one. It is said that it is the Ark of Nuh (peace be upon him), and the carrying of their offspring in it is the carrying of their earliest forefathers, who were in their loins, along with these people and their offspring. The singling out of their descendants for mention rather than them is because it is more eloquent in terms of favour, and more effective in producing the wonder upon which its being a sign revolves.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 42:

﴿And We have created for them from the like of it﴾ that which is similar to the ship, ﴿that they ride﴾ of the camels; for they are "ships of the land" (sufun al-barr). Or it means that which is similar to that ship, of boats and skiffs (zawarig). Their being made créated by Allah Most High, although they are among the handiworks of the servants, is not merely because their making is by the decrees (aqdar) and inspiration (ilham) of Allah Most High, but for the greater specificity of their origin to His power (qudra) and wisdom (hikma), as expressed by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes and Our revelation﴾. The expression of their association with these ships as "riding" is because they are by their own choice, just as the expression of their descendants' association with the ship of Noah, peace be upon him, is "carrying," because they were without their awareness and choice.

...(the rest of) the verse, part of the verse itself: they acknowledge its content, as His saying, exalted be He, expresses: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾. It was also read as (nugharriqahum), with the doubled ra' (the intensive form). Linking the drowning solely to His will indicates that what would necessitate their destruction, because of their sins, has been completed, and nothing remains except the attachment of His exalted will to it. That is: if We will, We drown them in the sea along with what We carried them in of the ship. The mention of the creation of camels at this point is a statement brought in the midst of the verse by way of istitrad (digression), given the complete similarity between camels and ships, as if camels were a kind of ship. Or the meaning is: along with what they ride of boats and skiffs. ﴿So there is no one to cry out for them﴾, i.e., no helper to protect them from drowning and to repel it from them before it occurs. It was said: "so there is no appeal for them," from their saying: "the one crying for help came to them." ﴿Nor are they rescued﴾, i.e., saved from it after it has occurred.

And His saying, exalted:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 44:**

﴿Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment﴾ is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exception in which the excluded element is left unstated, so the sentence is governed by the general sense of the preceding clause), taken from the most general of the causes, which encompasses both the motive that comes first and the purpose that comes later. That is: they are not rescued and not saved from anything except by a great mercy from Us, which calls for rescue and deliverance and for giving them enjoyment of life that follows from these two. It is also permissible that by "mercy" is meant what accompanies the enjoyment, namely worldly mercy, so that both become purposes of the rescue and deliverance. That is: for a kind of mercy and enjoyment ﴿for a time﴾, i.e., until a time whose term has been determined for them, as it has been said:

*"I did not submit in order to remain, but I was spared from fate only unto fate."*

﴿And when it is said to them, "Be mindful of"﴾ explains their turning away from the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyya), after the explanation of their turning away from the cosmic signs (al-ayat al-afaqiyya) that they were witnessing, and their failure to reflect upon them. That is: when it is said to them, by way of warning with what has been revealed of the signs or otherwise, "Be mindful of﴿ what is before you and what is behind you﴾" of the calamities and misfortunes, for they encompass you, or of the hardships that befall you from where you expect and from where you do not expect, or of the events that descended upon the nations before you and the punishment prepared for you in the Hereafter, or of the calamities of the heavens and the misfortunes of the earth, or of the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, or of the sins that preceded and those that follow. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw of "be mindful" or its purpose (ghaya), meaning: hoping that you will be shown mercy, or so that you will be shown mercy and thereby be saved from that, since you know that the basis of salvation is nothing but the mercy of God Most High. The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted, relying on its being understood from the saying of God Most High:

The meaning is clearly understood. If the warning is given by the noble verse itself, it is by the explicit wording (ʿibārat al-naṣṣ, the meaning derived directly from the words). If it is given by something other than the verse, it is by implication (dalālah). For since they turned away from the signs of their Lord, they would a fortiori turn away from other things, by way of greater priority (ṭarīq al-awlawiyyah, a fortiori reasoning). It is as if it were said: "When it is said to them, 'Beware of the punishment,' they turn away, as is their habit."

The word "مَا" is negative (nāfiyah). The form of the present tense (ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ) indicates continuous, renewed occurrence (al-istimrār al-tajaddudī). The first "مِن" is extra (mazīdah) to emphasise the generality of the noun, while the second "مِن" is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah) and, together with its governed noun, is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "آيَةٍ". The attribution of "الآياتِ" to the Name of the Lord, which is itself attributed to their pronoun ("رَبِّهِمْ"), serves to magnify its importance, which in turn entails magnifying the enormity of what they have dared to do against it.

By "the signs" is meant either the revealed verses (al-āyāt al-tanzīliyyah), so that "إتيانها" (their coming) means their descent, and the meaning is: no verse of the Qur'anic verses descends to them, among which are these verses that express what has been detailed of the marvels of God the Exalted's creation and the abundant blessings that call for turning towards them and believing in them, "إلّا كانُوا عَنْها مُعْرِضِينَ" (except that they turn away from them), in the manner of denial and mockery. Or it means what includes them and other signs of creation (al-āyāt al-takwīniyyah), which encompass miracles and other wonders of created things, among which are the three signs mentioned just above. In that case, "إتيانها" means what covers the descent of revelation and the manifestation of those matters to them. The meaning is: no sign appears to them from among the signs, among which is what has been mentioned of its affairs bearing witness to His oneness and His singularity in divinity, except that they turn away from it, abandoning the correct reflection upon it that would lead to belief in Him, the Exalted. The choice of this phrasing over "إلّا أعْرَضُوا عَنْها" (except that they turned away from it) is like what occurs in His saying: ﴿وَإنْ يَرَوْا آيَةً يُعْرِضُوا ويَقُولُوا سِحْرٌ مُسْتَمِرٌّ﴾ (And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"), to indicate their continuance in turning away in accordance with the continuance of the coming of the signs.

"عَنْ" is connected to "مُعْرِضِينَ" but was placed before it for the sake of the rhyming endings (al-fawāṣil). The clause is in the accusative position (fī ḥayyiz al-naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from the object of "تَأْتِي" or from its subject, which is specified by the description, because it contains a pronoun referring to each of them. The exception is an incomplete exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh) from the most general of states. That is: "ما تَأْتِيهِمْ مِن آيَةٍ مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِمْ" in any of their states except the state of their turning away from it; or: "ما تَأْتِيهِمْ آيَةٌ مِنها" in any of its states except the state of their turning away from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 47:

﴿And when it is said to them: Spend from what Allah has provided you﴾ That is: has given you, by way of bounty and favour, of various kinds of wealth. It is expressed in this way to affirm the truth, and to encourage spending in the manner of His saying, ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾, and to draw attention to the magnitude of their offence in failing to comply with the command. Likewise, "min" (from) is partitive (tab'idiyyah, indicating a part), meaning: when it is said to them, by way of counsel, "Spend some of what Allah the Exalted has given you of His bounty upon the needy" — for that is among the things that avert calamity and repel hardships — ﴿those who disbelieved said﴾ in the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, and they were zanadiqa (heretics) in Makkah, ﴿to those who believed﴾ in mockery of them, and in mockery of their habit of attributing matters to the will of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Shall we feed﴾ as you admonish us to do, ﴿him whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed﴾, that is: according to your claim.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: There were zanadiqa in Makkah who, when they were commanded to give charity to the poor, said: "No, by Allah! Shall Allah make him poor and we feed him?" It is also said: the polytheists of Quraysh said this when the poor among the believers asked them for food from their wealth, which they claimed they had dedicated to Allah the Exalted from the tilth and livestock. They implied that since Allah the Exalted did not will to feed them, though He is able to do so, then we are more entitled to that. This was nothing but the extreme of their ignorance, for Allah the Exalted feeds His servants through causes, among which is urging the rich to feed the poor and enabling them to do so. ﴿You are only in clear error﴾, in that you command us to do what contradicts the will of Allah the Exalted. It has also been permitted that this be a reply to them from Allah the Exalted, or a report of the answer of the believers to them.

And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" That is, regarding what you promise us of the Hour's establishment, addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, since they too used to recite to them the verses of warning about its coming. The meaning of "nearness" (qurb) here is either by way of mockery, or with regard to the nearness of the time of the promise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 49:

﴿What are they waiting for?﴾ This is a reply from Him, the Exalted, meaning: they are only waiting for ﴿a single blast﴾, which is the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula), ﴿that will seize them﴾ suddenly, ﴿while they are disputing﴾. That is, they are quarrelling over their trade and their dealings, and nothing of its signs comes to their minds. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized them suddenly while they did not perceive﴾. So they should not be deceived by the absence of its signs, nor claim that it will not come upon them. The original form of (yakhissimun) is (yakhtasimun): the ta' was made quiescent and assimilated into the sad, then the kha' was given a kasra because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. It is also read with a kasra on the ya' for the sake of harmony (lil-ittiba'), and with a fatha on the kha' by transferring the vowel of the ta' onto it. It is also read with the vowel reduced (ikhtilas), and with sukun, permitting the joining of two quiescent letters when the second is assimilated, even if the first is not a letter of prolongation (harf madd). It is also read (yakhsimun), from khasamahu, meaning when he argued with him.

Qur'anic quotations: "So they will not be able to make any bequest (tawsiyah)" in any of their affairs if they are among their families, "nor will they return to their families" if they are outside their doors. Rather, the Blast (al-Sayhah) will seize them suddenly, and they will die wherever they are.

﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾: this is the second blast, and between it and the first there are forty years. That is, it will be blown into; the past tense is used to indicate that the event is certain to occur. ﴿Then behold, they will rise from the graves (al-ajdath)﴾, that is, the tombs, the plural of jadath; it was also read with the letter fa' (فاء) [i.e., as "fa-idha" variant reading, "فَإِذَا" with fa' in place of the reading "فإذا" as written here]. ﴿To their Lord﴾, the Master of their affairs absolutely, ﴿they will hasten (yansiluna)﴾, that is, they will hurry, by way of compulsion and not by choice; this is based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"all of them will be brought before Us"﴾ [Qur'an 36:32]. It was also read with a dammah on the sin (ضم السين).

"They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?"" (The phrase is taken as a call to "Woe" to appear, since this is their time.) Recited also as "Woe to us" (with the accusative "wayla-tana"). "Who has raised us from our resting place?" Also recited as "man ahhabana" (from habba, "to wake from sleep" when one awakes), and as "man habbana," with the same meaning as ahhabana. It is said that the original was habba bina, and the preposition was dropped so that the verb reached the pronoun.

It is said: in this there is tarshih (an implicit hint and allusion), indicating that because their minds are confused, they imagine that they had been sleeping.

It is narrated from Mujahid that the disbelievers have a brief slumber in which they find the taste of sleep; so when the people of the graves are called, they say this.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on them all, that Allah Most High lifts the punishment from them between the two blasts (of the Trumpet), so they sleep; then when they are raised by the second blast and witness the terrors of the Resurrection that they witness, they call out "woe" and say this.

It is also said: when they see Hell and the various kinds of punishment in it, the punishment of the grave becomes, beside it, like sleep, so they say this.

It is recited as "min ba'thina" and "min habbina," with "min" as the preposition and the verbal noun. The word "marqad" is either a verbal noun, meaning "from our sleeping," or a noun of place used to denote the category, so it encompasses the resting places of all. "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truly" is a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), and "ma" is either a relative pronoun with its returning pronoun omitted, or a verbal-noun particle. This is an answer from the angels or from the believers, diverted from the usual pattern of their question, as a reminder of their disbelief, a rebuke to them for it, and an alert that what concerns them is asking about the resurrection itself—what it is—rather than about the one who raises them. As if they said: "The Most Merciful, who promised you this in His books and sent His messengers to you, who confirmed it, has raised you; the matter is not as you imagine, so as to ask about who raised you."

It is also said: this is from the speech of the disbelievers, as they recall what they heard from the messengers, peace be upon them, and answer themselves with it, or one another. It is also said: "This" is an attribute of "our resting place," and "what He promised..." to the end is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "what the Most Merciful promised and the messengers spoke truly is true."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 53:

﴿It was but one single shout﴾, i.e., the blast that was just related was nothing but ﴿one single shout﴾ produced by Israfil's—upon him be peace—blowing into the Trumpet (al-Sur). ﴿And behold, they are all brought up before Us﴾, i.e., gathered together, ﴿present﴾, without a delay of even the blink of an eye. In this there is, as is not hidden, a belittling of the matter of the Resurrection (al-ba'th) and the Gathering (al-hashr), and an indication that they are independent of causes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 54:

﴿So today no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ of souls, whether righteous or wicked, ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. That is: except the recompense for what you used to do in the world continuously, of disbelief and sins, by omitting the mudaf (the governed noun) and placing the mudaf ilayhi (the genitive noun) in its position, to alert to the strength of the mutual necessity and connection between them, as if they were one thing. Or [it means]: except with what you used to do, i.e., in return for it or because of it. The generalizing of the address to the believers is refuted by the fact that He, exalted is He, will pay them their wages and increase them from His bounty manifold. This is a report of what will be said to them when they see the punishment prepared for them, as a confirmation of the truth and a rebuke to them.

And the saying of the Exalted:

Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in delight, enjoying fruits. ﴿إنَّ أصْحابَ الجَنَّةِ اليَوْمَ في شُغُلٍ فاكِهُونَ﴾ is among what will be said to them on that Day, as an increase in their regret and remorse. The report of the good condition of their enemies right after the description of the evil condition of the disbelievers adds distress upon distress. This narrative is also a deterrent for these disbelievers from what they are upon, and an incentive to follow the way of the believers.

Shughl (busyness, occupation) is the matter that holds a person back and occupies him from his other affairs, because it is more important to him than all of them, either because it brings complete joy (al-masarrah) and delight (al-bahjah), or complete distress and grief. The intended meaning here is the first. The indefiniteness (al-tankir) and vagueness (al-ibham) in the word serve to indicate that it is too exalted to be described. What is meant by it is the various kinds of pleasures in which they are absorbed, which distract them completely from everything else.

As for the claim that it means the deflowering of virgins, or listening to music and the striking of strings, or mutual visiting, or the hospitality of Allah the Exalted, or that they are occupied from those in the Fire entirely, or that they are occupied from their families in the Fire, not concerned with their affairs and not caring for them, so that no disturbance enters their bliss, each of these has been reported from one of the great figures of the early generations (al-salaf). Their intention in this is not to restrict their busyness to what they mentioned alone, but to show that it is among their occupations. The singling out of each of them with mention of these matters is understood as required by the context of explanation. The phrase (fi shughl) together with its preposition is a predicate of inna, and fakihun is another predicate of it. That is: they are settled in busyness, and what busyness! In a busyness of great importance, enjoying everlasting bliss, attaining a great kingdom.

Expressing their state in this nominal sentence before it has come to pass, by treating what is awaited and expected as if it were already occurring, indicates the extreme speed of its realization and occurrence, and increases the distress of those addressed by it.

It is recited: (فِي شُغْلٍ) with a sukun on the ghayn, and (فِي شَغَلٍ) with two fathas, and with a fatha and a sukun. All are dialectal forms (lughat).

It is recited: (فَكِهُونَ) for emphasis (al-mubalaghah), and (فَكُهُونَ) with a damma on the kaf, which is a dialect like nutus. And (فاكِهِينَ) and (فَكِهِينَ) are in the accusative of state (al-hal) from the concealed pronoun (al-mustakinn) in the adverbial phrase (al-zarf).

And His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining on couches﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) brought to explain the manner of their occupation and enjoyment, and to complete it with what adds to their delight and joy: the companionship of their spouses with them, in what they are engaged in of occupation and pleasure. Grammatically, *hum* ("they") is the subject (*mubtada'*), *azwajuhum* ("their spouses") is conjoined to it (*'atf*), and *muttaki'un* ("reclining") is the predicate (*khabar*). The two prepositional phrases are complements of it (*silatan lahu*), placed before it for the sake of observing the verse endings (*fawasil*, the rhyming pauses of the verses). Alternatively, *muttaki'un* together with the two prepositional phrases attached to it by the sense of settledness (*istiqrar*) form successive predicates. It has also been said that the predicate is the first adverbial phrase, and the second is a resumed clause, connected to *muttaki'un*, which is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has also been said that it is a fronted predicate, with *muttaki'un* as a delayed subject. It is recited as *muttakin* without the hamza, in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun implied in the two adverbial phrases or one of them. It has also been said that *hum* is an emphatic reinforcement of the pronoun in the predicate of *inna*, with *muttaki'un* as another predicate of it, and *'ala al-ara'ik* is connected to it; likewise *fi zilal*, or this is governed by a hidden verb and is a state (*hal*) of the two conjoined nouns.

*Zilal* is the plural of *zill*, like *shi'ab* is the plural of *sha'b*, or the plural of *zullah*, like *qibab* is the plural of *qubbah*. This is supported by the recitation *fi zullal*. *Ara'ik* is the plural of *arika*, which is a couch adorned with garments and curtains. Tha'lab said: "An *arika* is not one unless there is a canopy (*hajlah*) over it."

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 57:

﴿Theirs therein is fruit﴾ ... etc. It is an explanation of what they enjoy in Paradise of food and drink, and what they take delight in of physical and spiritual pleasures, after the explanation of the gatherings of intimacy and assemblies of holiness that they have therein, as a completion of the explanation of the manner of their occupation and joy. That is: theirs therein is abundant fruit of every kind of fruit. And (mā) in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and theirs is whatever they request﴾ is either a relative pronoun (mawsūlah) or a qualifying noun (mawṣūfah), and it is used to refer to a called-for (object) of great importance, specific or unspecified, signifying that it alone is worthy of being requested to the exclusion of anything else; then it is stated explicitly, for the sake of increasing the affirmation with confirmation after the arousing of longing, as you will come to know; or it remains on its generality, intended for generalization after the specification of some of the customary items by mention. Whatever the case, it is a subject (mubtada'), and "lahum" (theirs) is its predicate, and the sentence is conjoined to the preceding sentence. And not being content with conjoining "mā yaddaʿūna" (whatever they request) to "fākihah" (fruit) is so that it is not supposed that "mā" refers to the accessories and complements of the fruit.

And the meaning: theirs is whatever they request for themselves from a called-for object of great importance; or, whatever they request, of whatever kind, of the causes of joy and the occasions of delight. Whatever the case, it contains an indication that they are at the utmost extent of joy and felicity. And (yaddaʿūna) is a form of (yafta'ilūna) from the root "du'ā'" (calling/requesting), as has been indicated, like (ishtawā) and (ijtamala) meaning "he roasted" and "he gathered for himself"; and it has been said: it means "yatadā'ūna" (they call to one another), like "irtamā" meaning "tarāmī" (throwing at one another); and it has been said: it means "yatamannawna" (they wish), from their saying: "ud'u 'alayya mā shi'ta" (call down upon me whatever you wish), meaning "tamannahu 'alayya" (wish it for me).

And al-Zajjaj said: it is from the du'ā' (request), i.e., what the people of Paradise call for, it comes to them; so the iftiʿāl form is in the sense of the simple verb, like "ihtimāl" in the sense of "ḥiml" and "irtiḥāl" in the sense of "ruḥlah"; and the reading with the lightened form (taḫfīf) supports it, as al-Kawashi mentioned.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 58:

﴿Salamun﴾ (peace). On the first interpretation, it is either a substitution (badal) for "what they call for" (ma yaddaʿūna), or the predicate of an omitted subject. The statement of the Exalted, ﴿qawlan﴾ (a word), is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar muʾakkid) for an implied verb, and it is a qualifier (sifah) of "salamun." What follows it, the prepositional phrase, is connected to an implied verb which is a qualifier of it. It is as if it were said: "For them there is peace," or "What they call for is peace; it is said to them, a word coming ﴿from﴾ ﴿a Lord, Most Merciful﴾," meaning: greetings are conveyed to them from Him, exalted is He, through the angel or without him, as an expression of honouring them. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The angels enter upon them with the greeting from the Lord of the worlds."

As for the second interpretation, it has been said that it is the predicate of "what they call for," and "lahum" (for them) serves to specify the recipient, as one says: "For Zayd, nobility is abundant," where "nobility" is the subject and "abundant" is its predicate, and the prepositional phrase specifies to whom it belongs. That is: "What they call for is sound, pure for them, without any admixture." In this case "qawlan" is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the sentence, that is: "a promise from a Lord, Most Merciful." The more apt view is that it is in the accusative of specification (ikhtisas). It has also been said that it is a subject with an omitted predicate, meaning: "For them there is peace," that is: greeting, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful, or safety from calamities; in that case "qawlan" is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the sentence, as has preceded.

It has been said that its implied form is "salamun ʿalayhim" (peace upon them), in which case it is a report of what will be said to them from Him, exalted is He, on that Day. It has also been said that its predicate is the implied verb governing "qawlan" as its object, and it has been said that its predicate is "min rabbin raḥīm" (from a Lord, Most Merciful). It has been read as "salaman" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning: for them is what they desire, sound and pure. It has also been read as "silmun," which has the same meaning as "salam" in both senses.

﴿And separate yourselves today﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf), either coordinated with the preceding sentence, which is brought to explain the conditions of the people of Paradise. This does not mean that the intended object is the imperative verb itself, such that one would have to contrive a suitable item for it to be coordinated with.
