Rather, it is the coordination of the account of the bad condition of these people and the manner of their punishment with the account of the good condition of those people and the description of their reward, as occurred in His exalted saying: ﴿And give good news to those who believe﴾ ... the verse. It seems that the change in the arrangement of the discourse was to evoke the complete contrast between the two groups and their two states. Or it is coordinated with an implied element (idmar) to which the narration of the condition of the people of Paradise leads, as if it were said, after explaining that they are occupied with a matter of great importance and that they have attained a lasting bliss that speech falls short of describing: "So let them be comforted by this, and separate yourselves from them, ﴿O guilty ones﴾, toward your destination."

From Qatada: "Withdraw from every good." From al-Dahhak: "For every disbeliever there is a house of the Fire in which he neither sees nor is seen."

As for what has been said, that the implied element is "then let them separate," it is far from correct, because the ones being spoken of do not have as their destiny the praiseworthy state mentioned, so that the stated command could be made to follow from it. Rather, their actual state is their steady remaining in it. That this is by way of treating the awaited as if it were already realized does not benefit, because the basis for implying an element is that the minds are led toward it and the structure of the speech is directed toward it. Once that state has been treated as already actual, due to the brilliant subtlety and wonderful wisdom that the context required, as has been explained, and its being awaited has been entirely removed from the level of consideration, then undertaking to imply something that relates to it would take the noble composition completely out of its eloquence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 60:

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾ — this is part of what will be said to them by way of rebuke, reproach and silencing, between the command to separate themselves (from the believers) and the command to enter Hell, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Burn therein today﴾ ... etc. The ʿahd (covenant, charge) is an injunction and a prior directive containing good and benefit. What is meant here is what God Most High imposed upon them through the tongues of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, of commands and prohibitions, among which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan seduce you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾ ... the verse, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, and other noble verses that occur in this meaning.

It has been said: it is the covenant taken from them when they were brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam and called to bear witness against themselves.

It has been said: it is the proofs established for them, both rational and transmitted (samʿiyya), commanding them to worship Him, exalted is He, and forbidding them to worship other than Him. What is meant by "worshipping Satan" is obedience to him in what he whispers to them and makes attractive to them. It is expressed as "worship" to intensify the warning and aversion from it, in contrast to the worship of Him, mighty and majestic is He.

It was also read as (iʿhad) with a kasra on the hamza, as (aʿhid) with a kasra on the ha', as (aḥhad) with a ḥa' in place of the ʿayn, and as (aḥḥad) with idgham (assimilation), and this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, i.e., manifest in enmity. This is a justification for the obligation to desist from what is forbidden. It has also been said that it is a justification for the prohibition itself.

﴿And that you worship Me﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "that you do not worship" (أنْ لا تَعْبُدُوا), on the basis that the "أن" in both is interpretive (mufassira) of the covenant (ʿahd), which carries the sense of saying with a prohibition and a command. Or it is a verbal "أن" (maṣdariyya) from which the preposition has been dropped, meaning: Did I not charge you concerning abandoning the worship of Satan and concerning worshipping Me? The placing of the prohibition before the command is because the clearing away (takhliya) of what is false has priority over the adorning (taḥliya) with what is true, as in the statement of tawhid. It is also so that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿This is a straight path﴾ follows it, for it refers to His worship, which is an expression for tawhid and Islam, and it is what is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿This is a straight path upon Me﴾. The intended meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ is the same, and the indefiniteness (tankīr) is for magnification (tafkhīm). And the lām in His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 62:

﴿And indeed he led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. It is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam mahdhuf), and the sentence is a resumptive clause (istie'naf) brought to intensify the reproach and to emphasize the rebuke, by showing that their transgressions were not merely the breaking of the covenant but also including their failure to take warning from the punishments that fell upon the earlier nations because of their obedience to Satan. Thus the address is to their later generations, among whom are the disbelievers of Makkah, who are singled out for added reproach and rebuke because their transgressions had multiplied.

Al-Jibill (with a kasra on the jim and the ba', and a shaddah on the lam) means creation (al-khalq). It has been read with two dammas and a shaddah, with two dammas and no shaddah, with a damma and a sukun, with two kasras and no shaddah, and with a kasra and a sukun; all of these are dialectal forms (lughat).

It has also been read as (jiblan), the plural of jibla, like fitr and khalq in the sense of fitrah and khilqah (natural disposition and created constitution). It has been read as (jilan) with a ya', meaning a category or kind of people. The meaning is: and by Allah, he indeed led astray from among you a great creation, or a great category (p-176) [of people], away from that straight path which I commanded you to remain steadfast upon. Consequently there befell them what befell them of the terrible punishments whose reports filled the horizons and whose traces remained through the ages.

The "fa" in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ is for conjunction (li'l-'atf) upon an implied element required by the context, meaning: Were you witnessing the traces of their punishments, and yet you did not use your reason to understand that they were due to their misguidance? Or: Did you not use your reason at all, so that you would desist from what they were upon, lest the punishment befall you?

And the saying of the Exalted:

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 63:

﴿This is Hell which you were promised.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (istie'naf), addressed to them after the completion of the rebuke, reproach, censure and reproof, when they stand at the brink of Hell. That is: you were promised it through the tongues of the Messengers, peace be upon them, in return for worshipping Satan, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and those who follow you, all together.﴾ And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Go, and whoever follows you among them, indeed Hell is your recompense, an ample recompense."﴾ And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Get out of it, reviled and expelled. Whoever follows you among them – I will surely fill Hell with you all."﴾ And other than that, which cannot be counted.

And His saying, the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 64:

﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ This is a command of humiliation and degradation, like His saying: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble.﴾ ... etc. That is: enter it from above, and experience the various kinds of its torment today because of your persistent disbelief in the world.

And His saying, exalted is He:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 65:**

﴿Today We shall seal their mouths.﴾ That is, a seal that prevents them from speaking. The shift to the third person (*iltifat*, a shift in grammatical person) indicates that mentioning their repulsive conditions calls for turning away from them and describing their dreadful state to others. This also implies that the sealing is among the requirements of the situation, since address is for receiving a reply, and that has been entirely cut off. It has also been read as (تَخْتِمُ) [*takhtimu*, "You seal"].

﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾ It is narrated that they will deny and dispute, so their neighbours, their families and their clans will bear witness against them, and they will swear that they were not polytheists. Then their mouths will be sealed, and their hands and feet will speak.

It is stated in a hadith: "The servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'I do not accept any witness against me except myself.' So his mouth will be sealed, and his limbs will be told, 'Speak!' and they will speak of his deeds. Then he will be left free to speak, and he will say: 'Away with you, may you be destroyed! It was on your account that I was contending.'"

It has also been said that the speaking of the limbs and their testimony means that they indicate their actions, and that the traces of sins appear upon them. It has been read as (وَتَتَكَلَّمُ أيْدِيهِمْ) [*wa-tatakallamu aydihim*, "and their hands speak"]. It has also been read as (وَلِتُكَلِّمَنا أيْدِيهِمْ وتَشَهُدَ) with the lam of purpose and the accusative (naṣb) mood, meaning: "and for that reason We seal their mouths." And it has been read as (وَلْتُكَلِّمْنا أيْدِيهِمْ ولْتَشْهَدْ) with the lam of command and the jussive (jazm) mood, meaning: "and let their hands speak to Us, and let their feet bear witness."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 66:

﴿And if We willed, We would surely have obliterated their eyes﴾ Al-tams (obliteration) is effacing the slit of the eye until it becomes smooth and wiped over (mamsuhah). The object of the will (al-mashi'ah) is omitted according to the established rule, which is that its occurrence as a condition, and the fact that its object is the content of the consequent, i.e.: if We willed to obliterate their eyes, We would have done it. The choice of the future form (sighat al-istiqbal), although the meaning is past, is to convey that the non-obliteration of their eyes is due to the continued absence of the will; for the negated present tense (al-mudari' al-manfi) occupying the place of the past is not explicit in conveying the cessation of the continuation of the act (p-177), but may convey the continuation of its negation according to the context, as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if God were to hasten evil upon mankind as they seek to hasten good﴾ ﴿and they raced to the path﴾, i.e.: they intended to race towards the road they were accustomed to travel, on the basis that its accusative case is by removal of the preposition; or it is by implying the sense of hastening (al-ibtidar) in racing (al-istibaq), or by the adverbial sense (al-zarfiyyah). ﴿Then how could they see﴾ the path and the direction of travel?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 67:

﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them﴾ by changing their forms and nullifying their powers, ﴿in their place﴾, that is, in their place. However, the word makana (مَكانَة) is more specific, like maqama (مَقامَة) and maqam (مَقام). It is also read as ﴿'alā makānātihim﴾ (in their places), meaning: We would have transformed them into a transformation that freezes them in their place, so that they cannot move away from it, whether by advancing, retreating, or returning. This is the meaning of His Exalted saying: ﴿So they would not be able to proceed, nor would they return﴾, that is, nor would they return; the verb was placed in its position to maintain the rhyme (fāṣila).

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: monkeys and swine.

It was also said: stones.

From Qatada: We would have made them sit on their feet and paralysed them.

It is also read as (miḍiyyan) with a kasra and a fatha on the mim. The two conditional clauses are not merely to state God's power over what was mentioned of the punishment of obliteration and transformation. Rather, they show that they, by what they are upon of disbelief, breaking the covenant, and failing to take warning from what they witnessed of the ruin of their like, are deserving that this punishment be inflicted upon them in this world, just as the punishment of sealing was inflicted upon them in the Hereafter. And that what prevents this is nothing but the non-attachment of the Divine will to it. As if it were said: If We willed to punish them with what was mentioned, of obliteration and transformation, in accordance with the requirement of their crimes which call for it, We would have done it; but We did not will it, in accordance with the ways of mercy and wisdom which call for granting them respite.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 68:

﴿And whomever We cause to live long, We reverse him in creation﴾ i.e., We prolong his life, ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾ i.e., We turn him over within it and create him in the opposite of how We created him at first, so that his weakness continually increases, his strength diminishes, his physique is reduced, and his form and appearance change, until he returns to a state resembling the condition of a child in the weakness of the body, the lack of intellect, and the absence of understanding and perception. It has also been read as (nankusuhu) from the unaugmented triliteral form, and (nunkisuhu) from the causative form (al-inkas).

﴿Will they not then use their intellect?﴾ i.e., do they see this and yet not understand that the One who is able to do this is able to do what has been mentioned of obliteration and transformation, and that the non-occurrence of these two is due to the non-attachment of His, the Exalted's, will to them? (ta'qilun) is read with the letter ta' because the address preceding it is in the second person.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 69:

﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ is a rejection and refutation of what they used to say about him ﷺ, that he is a poet and that what he recites is poetry. That is, We did not teach him poetry through the teaching of the Qur'an, in the sense that the Qur'an is not poetry. For poetry is contrived speech, fabricated and ornamented, a composed discourse woven to the pattern of metre and rhyme, built upon imaginings and feeble illusions. Where is that from the sublime and weighty revelation, free from resemblance to the speech of mankind, filled with varied wisdoms and wondrous rulings that lead to the happiness of this world and the Hereafter? And how did their affairs become confused, and their suppositions become mixed up? ﴿May Allah destroy them; how are they turned away?﴾

﴿And it is not befitting for him﴾: that poetry would not be proper for him, and would not be attainable for him even if he sought it. That is, We made him such that if he wanted to compose poetry, it would not be possible for him, just as We made him unlettered, unable to guide himself to writing, so that the proof would be more established and the doubt more easily refuted.

As for his ﷺ saying:

> "I am the Prophet, there is no falsehood in it; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib."

and his ﷺ saying:

> "Are you not but a finger that bled, and what you suffered in the way of Allah?"

these fall under the category of coincidences that occur without intention to them and without resolve to arrange them.

It is also said: the pronoun in "lahu" (for him) refers to the Qur'an, meaning: it is not befitting for the Qur'an to be poetry. ﴿It is not but﴾, that is, the Qur'an is not but ﴿a reminder﴾, that is, an admonition from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and guidance for both humans and jinn, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾. ﴿And a clear Qur'an﴾, that is, a heavenly book whose being such is evident, or one that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, which is read in the prayer niches, recited in places of worship, and through its recitation and acting upon what is in it, the success of both abodes is attained. How far is it, then, from what they said?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 70:

﴿That he may warn﴾ i.e., the Qur'an, or the Messenger (ﷺ). The reading with the letter ta' (لِتُنْذِرَ) supports this. It was also read (لِيَنْذُرَ) from nadhara bihi, meaning "he knew of it," and (لِيُنْذَرَ) in the passive voice from al-indhar (warning). ﴿Whoever is alive﴾ i.e., possessed of intellect and reflection, for the heedless is like the dead. Or: a believer in the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, for eternal life is through faith. The specification of warning to such a person is because he is the one who benefits from it. ﴿And the word may be fulfilled﴾ i.e., the word of punishment may be justified ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, those who persist in disbelief. The mention of them in contrast to "whoever is alive" implies that, lacking the traces of life and its rulings, which are knowledge, they are in reality dead.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 71:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denial and wonder, and the waw is for conjunction with a suppressed negative sentence implied by the conjoined clause, i.e., "Have they not reflected, or not taken notice, and not known with a certain knowledge bordering on direct witnessing?" ﴿That We have created for them﴾ i.e., for their sake and benefit, ﴿from what Our hands have made﴾ i.e., from what We Ourselves undertook to bring into being directly. The mention of the hands and the attribution of the work to them is a metaphor conveying an intensification of exclusiveness and singularity in originating it and of special care for it. ﴿cattle﴾ is the object of (created), and its being placed after the two prepositional phrases attached to it, although its proper place is before them, is for the reason that has been mentioned many times: the attention given to what is put first and the arousing of anticipation for what is put last. For what should be first, when delayed, leaves the soul awaiting it, so that when it arrives it settles in more firmly, especially when the fronted element indicates that the delayed element is a beneficial and momentous matter, as in the noble arrangement here. The first prepositional phrase, which expresses that the delayed item is among their benefits, and the second, which makes clear that it is among momentous matters, increase the soul's yearning for it and desire for it. Also, in delaying it there is a joining of it with its consequences that follow by the words of the Exalted: ﴿so they are its owners﴾, i.e., the three verses. That is, "We made them its possessors." The choice of the nominal sentence over that is to indicate the stability and continuity of their ownership of them. The lam is connected to (owners) and reinforces its governing force, i.e., "they are owners of them through Our making them owners of them, disposing of them independently, exclusively benefiting from them, none sharing that with them; or they are able to control them, empowered to dispose of them by Our decree, Our enablement and Our subjecting them to them," as in the words of one who said:

Ṣ I have become one who carries no weapon, and I do not own the head of a camel if it bolts.

The first is the more apparent, so that the Exalted saying:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 72:**

﴿And We have subjugated them to them﴾ — (this is) an establishing of a blessing in its own right, not a continuation of what precedes it; that is, We made them (the cattle) submissive to them, such that they do not resist them in anything they wish to do with them, including slaughtering (p-179), as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Some of them they ride﴾ ... and so on, for the *fa'* (fa) in it is for deriving the rulings of the subjugation from it and detailing them. That is: some of them are their mount (rukubuhum), i.e., their means of riding; that is, most of their benefit is riding. The lack of mention of carrying (loads) is because it is among the complements of riding.

It is also read as (rakubatuhum), which has the same meaning as *halub* and *halubah* (a milch animal); and it has been said that *rakubah* is a collective noun. It is also read as (rukubuhum), meaning: possessing their riding. ﴿And of them they eat﴾ — that is: and some of them they eat, its meat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 73:

﴿And for them therein﴾ — that is, in the cattle, both kinds of them — ﴿are benefits﴾ other than riding and eating, such as hides, wool and fur, and other things, and [such as] plowing with the bulls, ﴿and drinks﴾ from the milk — the plural of mashrab (drinking-place, here meaning drink). This is a summary of what was detailed in Surah al-Nahl. ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ — that is: do they witness these blessings, or do they enjoy them and yet not thank the One who bestowed them?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 74:

﴿And they took besides Allah⁠﴾ — i.e., transgressing Allah, the Exalted, whose sole possession of that overwhelming power they had witnessed, and whose bounty upon them in those manifold blessings they had seen — ﴿gods﴾ from among the idols, and they associated them with Him, exalted is He, in worship. ﴿Perhaps they would be helped⁠﴾ — hoping that they would be helped by them in what befell them of affairs, or that they would intercede for them in the Hereafter.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 75:

﴿They are not able to help them﴾ ... etc. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain the invalidity of their opinion, the frustration of their hope, and the reversal of their scheme. That is: their gods are not able to help them. ﴿And they﴾, i.e., the polytheists, ﴿for them﴾, i.e., for their gods, ﴿are an army brought forward (muhdarun)﴾, who escort them when they are driven to the Fire. It was also said: they are prepared in the world (mu'addun fi al-dunya) for their protection, service, and defense, but the context of the noble composition does not support this, for the fa' in His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 76:

﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾. This is for the arrangement of the prohibition upon what precedes it, so it must be an expression of their loss and their deprivation of what they hoped for in their empty expectations, and the reversal of the matter upon them, by the ordaining of evil upon what they had arranged in hope of good. For that is among the things that make the affair easier and bring consolation.

As for their being prepared to serve and guard them, that is far removed from this. The prohibition, although on the surface it is directed at their speech, is in reality directed at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and is a prohibition to him, peace be upon him, against being affected by it, by way of kinaya (metonymy) in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. For the prohibition of the causes of a thing and its origins that lead to it is a prohibition of the thing itself by way of demonstrative proof, and a negation of its causal connection.

The prohibition may be directed at the effect while what is meant is a prohibition of the cause, as in his saying:

﴿Never let me see you here﴾

He means by it a prohibition to the one addressed against being present before him. What is meant by "their speech" is what is indicated by the mention of their taking idols as gods, for that cannot be free of uttering their saying: "These are our gods," and that they are partners of Allah, glorified is He, in worship, and other things of this kind that bring grief.

It is also read (yuhzinka) with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, from aḥzana (to cause grief), which is the transitive form derived from ḥazina (to grieve), the intransitive.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We know what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ is an explicit rationale for the prohibition, by way of resumption (istiʼnāf), after its rationale was given by way of indication. For knowledge of what has been mentioned necessarily entails requital with certainty; that is, We will requite them for all their crimes, both hidden and manifest, none of which escapes Our knowledge. In this there is an excellent consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The mention of the secret before the open is either for emphasis in declaring the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all knowable things, as though His knowledge of what they conceal is prior to His knowledge of what they reveal, although in reality the two are equal, for His knowledge of His objects is not by way of the acquisition of their forms; rather, the existence of each thing in itself is knowledge in relation to Him, and in this sense the situation does not differ between things that are manifest and things that are hidden. Or it is because the rank of the secret precedes the rank of the open, since there is nothing that is made open except that it, or its origins, is concealed in the heart before that; so His knowledge's connection to its first state precedes its connection to its second state in reality.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 77:

﴿Have not seen man that We created him from a drop [of semen]?﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to explain the falsity of their denial of resurrection, after they had witnessed within themselves its clearest proofs and most just testimonies; just as what preceded it was brought to explain the falsity of their associating others with Allah, the Exalted, after they had seen in what was in their hands that which necessitates tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and Islam.

As for what has been said, that it is a second consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by belittling what they say regarding their denial of the gathering (al-hashr), then no. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denial and wonder, and the waw is for conjunction, coordinating with an implied sentence which the following clause is made to follow, as occurred in the earlier denial sentence. That is: "Did man not reflect, and did he not know with certain knowledge ﴿that We created him from a drop [of semen]﴾ ... and so on?" Or it is the very same earlier sentence repeated as an emphasis of the previous rebuke and as a preparation for denying what is more deserving of denial and wonder. This is because what was denied there was their lack of knowledge of what relates to the creation of the means of their livelihoods, whereas here it is their lack of knowledge of what relates to the creation of their own selves. There is no doubt that a person's knowledge of his own condition is more important, and his comprehension of it is easier and more complete; so denial and wonder at the neglect of that are more fitting. It is as if it were said: "Did they not know that He, the Exalted, created the means of their livelihoods, and did they not also know that He, the Exalted, created them for their own selves? Even though knowledge of that is most evident and of the utmost importance," meaning that the first denial is remote and ugly, and the second is more remote and uglier.

It is also permissible that the waw is for conjoining the second denial sentence to the first, on the basis that the first is prior in consideration, and that the hamza's precedence over it is because it requires initial position in the sentence, as is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). The mention of "man" (al-insan) in the position of a pronoun is because the basis of the denial relates to his conditions insofar as he is a human being, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam 19:67].

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿then behold, he is a clear adversary﴾, meaning: intensely contentious and argumentative in falsehood, it is conjoined to the negative clause and falls within the scope of denial and wonder, as if it were said: "Has he not seen that We created him from the basest and most contemptible of things, and then, behold, he opposes Us in a matter whose truth and certainty the origin of his own natural creation testifies to, with a clear testimony?" The use of a nominal sentence indicates his firm establishment in contention and his persistence in it.

It is narrated that a group of the Quraysh disbelievers, among them Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, Abu Jahl, al-As ibn Wa'il and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, discussed this matter. Ubayy ibn Khalaf said to them: "Do you not see what Muhammad says, that Allah resurrects the dead?" Then he said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will go to him and dispute with him!" He took a decayed bone and began crumbling it with his hand, saying: "O Muhammad, does Allah think He will give life to this after it has become dust?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and admit you into Hell." Then this was revealed.

It is also said: the meaning of the Exalted's words ﴿then behold, he is a clear adversary﴾ is: then behold, he, after having been a despised fluid, is a distinguishing, articulate man, capable of disputation, clearly expressing what is in himself, eloquent. In that case it is conjoined to (khalaqnahu, "We created him"), not falling under the denial and wonder, but rather being one of the completing proofs of the soundness of resurrection.

(p-181) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he sets forth for Us a parable﴾ is then coordinated with the negative sentence and falls within the scope of denunciation and reproach. As for the first interpretation, it is coordinated with the sentence of suddenness, and the meaning is: "he was suddenly confronted with our dispute and set forth for us a parable," that is, he brought forward concerning us a story that is in reality strange, and in its strangeness and remoteness from the intellects it is like a parable, namely the denial of Our reviving the bones. Or it is a story that he considered strange, which he deemed remote and classed among parables, and denied most vehemently, namely Our reviving it. He made for Us a parable and an equal from creation, measured Our power by their power, and negated the whole in general.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And forgets his creation﴾ means: Our creating him in the aforementioned manner, which indicates the falsity of what he set forth. It is either coordinated with (set forth), falling within the scope of denunciation and wonder, or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to its subject, with *qad* implied or not implied.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He says﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) that came as an answer to a question arising from the narration of his setting forth a parable, as if it were said: "What parable was set forth, or what did he say?" So it was said: "He says: ﴿Who will give life to the bones﴾," denying it in the strongest terms, and emphasizing it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they are decayed﴾, that is, crumbling to the utmost degree of decay, most remote from life in the extreme.

So the parable, on the first view, is the denial of His, exalted is He, giving life to the bones, for it is a matter that is in reality strange, and by its strangeness and remoteness from the intellects it is fit to be counted a parable, since the intellects firmly judge the denial to be false and the denied matter to occur, as it is like origination (inshā') or even easier than it in the measure of reason.

On the second view, it is His, exalted is He, giving life to them, for it is a matter that is strange in his opinion; he deemed it remote, counted it among parables, and denied it most vehemently, although it is in reality closer than anything to occurrence, because of what has preceded, namely that it is like origination, or easier than it.

As for the third view, there is no difference whether the parable is the denial or the denied matter. The non-feminization of *ramīm*, despite its being a predicate of a feminine subject, is because it is a noun for what has decayed of the bones, not an adjective, like *rufāt* (crumbs). Whoever affirmed life for the bone has held fast to the apparent meaning of this noble verse and built upon it the ruling of the impurity of the bone of a carrion animal. As for our companions, they do not say that bone has life, as hair does not; they say that what is meant by reviving the bones is returning them to the freshness and moistness they had in a living, sensitive body.

**[Say]** as a rebuke to him, by reminding him of what he had attributed to his own creation, which points to the reality of the matter, and by guiding him to the method of reasoning from it: ﴿He will give them life who produced them the first time﴾. For His power is as it is, since change is impossible in it, and the substance remains in its state. ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾, being exceedingly thorough in knowledge of the details of the manner of creating and originating, both in production and in restoration. He encompasses all the scattered and dispersed parts of each individual person, their roots and branches, and the states of some of them in relation to others, in joining and separation, in gathering and dispersal. So He restores each of these in the pattern that preceded, with the same powers that were there before.

The clause is either a concluding parenthetical statement (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) that confirms the content of the answer, or it is conjoined to the relative clause (ṣilah). The shift to a nominal sentence serves to alert the listener that His knowledge of what has been mentioned is a continuous attribute, unlike His act of bringing creatures into being.

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 80:

﴿Who has made for you, from the green tree, fire﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first relative pronoun (al-mawsul al-awwal). The reason it is not sufficient to conjoin its relative clause to the other relative clause (ʿataf) is for emphasis, and because the two differ in the manner of signification; that is, He created for your sake and benefit from it fire. This is on the basis that the making (al-ja'l) is originative (ibda'i). The two prepositional phrases (al-jarran) are connected to it and have been placed before its explicit object, though they are ranked after it, because of the concern with what is placed first (al-i'tina' bil-muqaddam) and the arousing of eagerness for what comes later (al-tashwiq ila al-mu'akhkhar), as has already passed.

The description of the tree as "green" (akhdar) is in view of the wording (al-lafz). It has also been read as "al-khadra'" (green, feminine) in view of the meaning (al-ma'na). It refers to the marikh and the 'ifar, from which a man cuts two sticks like miswaks, and they are green, moisture dripping from them. He grinds the marikh, which is male, upon the 'ifar, which is female, and fire is struck by God's permission, the Exalted. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then, from it, you kindle﴾. So whoever is able to bring fire forth from the green tree, despite the watery nature contrary to it in its quality, is more able to restore freshness to what was fresh, and then dryness and decay befell it.

And His saying, the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 81:

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth…﴾ … etc. This is a resumptive statement (istinaf) issued from Him, Mighty and Majestic, to establish the content of the answer which he (ﷺ) was commanded to address to them with this, and to impose the proof upon them. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denunciation and negation, and the waw is for conjunction upon an implied element required by the context. That is: "Is not He who originated them the first time, and is not He who made for them fire from the green tree, and is not He who created the heavens and the earth – despite their great bulk and the magnitude of their station – ﴿able to create the like of them﴾ in smallness and insignificance relative to them? For the immediate judgment of reason dictates that whoever is able to create them is even more able to create human beings, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Certainly the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾." It was also read as (yaqdiru).

His words, exalted be He, ﴿Yes (bala)﴾ are an answer from His side, and an explicit statement of what the denunciatory interrogation conveyed of affirming what follows the negation, and a notice that the answer is determined; whether they spoke it or stammered over it for fear of being held to it. His words, exalted be He, ﴿And He is the Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ are a conjunction upon what the affirmation conveys, that is: "Yes, He is able to do that, and He is the one who is extreme in creating and in knowledge, in quality and in quantity."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 82:

﴿Indeed, His command﴾ i.e., His affair ﴿when He intends a thing﴾ among things ﴿is only that He says to it, "Be!"﴾ i.e., that He attaches His power to it ﴿and it is﴾ so it comes into being without depending on anything else at all. This is an illustration of His, exalted is He, power over what He wills, by the command of a commanding ruler to an obeyed subordinate, regarding the swiftness with which the commanded thing is achieved, without depending on anything whatsoever. And it has been read (fa-yakūna) in the accusative, as a conjunction with (yaqūla).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 36, verse 83:**

﴿So glorified is He in whose hand is the sovereignty (malakut) of everything﴾. It is a declaration of His transcendence, exalted and sublime, above what they have attributed to Him, and an expression of wonder at what they have said concerning Him, may He be exalted. The meaning of "subhan" (glorification, the declaration that God is exempt from every imperfection) has already been verified. The "fa" (so) indicates that what has been detailed of His affairs necessitates His transcendence and the declaration of it with the most complete necessity. Likewise, describing Him as the Owner in an absolute and comprehensive sense indicates that this ownership necessitates that transcendence with the most complete necessitation. "Malakut" is an intensive form of "mulk" (dominion), like "rahamut" and "rahbut".

It was also read as "malikat kulli shay'" (مَلِكَةُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ), "mamlakat kulli shay'" (مَمْلَكَةُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ) and "mulk kulli shay'" (مُلْكُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ). ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, not to anyone else. It was also read as "turji'un" (تَرْجِعُونَ) with a fatha on the ta' from "ruju'" (return). In it is a promise and a warning that is not hidden.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, he said: "I did not know what has been narrated concerning the virtues of Ya-Sin and reciting it, how it was singled out for that, until I found that it is due to this verse."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites it, desiring thereby the Face of Allah, the Exalted, Allah will forgive him, and he will be given a reward as if he had recited the Qur'an twenty-two times. And any Muslim before whom it is recited when the Angel of Death has descended upon him, [it is Ya-Sin]."
